assertions.source_quote: This review compares the original Vision Transformer (ViT) with convolutional neural-network backbones used as visual feature extractors. The organizing choice is to separate architecture and inductive bias from the training regime and downstream task: ViT is a convolution-free sequence model over fixed image patches, whereas CNN backbones such as ResNet and ResNeXt build image representations through stacked local convolutions whose effective receptive fields grow with depth. This distinction matters because ViT's headline result was not that transformers universally dominate CNNs under every setup; it was that, when pretrained on large data and transferred to ImageNet, CIFAR-100, VTAB and other recognition benchmarks, a pure patch-transformer could match or exceed strong convolutional networks while using substantially fewer computational resources to train. assertions.source_quote: This review compares the original Vision Transformer (ViT) with convolutional neural-network backbones used as visual feature extractors. The organizing choice is to separate architecture and inductive bias from the training regime and downstream task: ViT is a convolution-free sequence model over fixed image patches, whereas CNN backbones such as ResNet and ResNeXt build image representations through stacked local convolutions whose effective receptive fields grow with depth. This distinction matters because ViT's headline result was not that transformers universally dominate CNNs under every setup; it was that, when pretrained on large data and transferred to ImageNet, CIFAR-100, VTAB and other recognition benchmarks, a pure patch-transformer could match or exceed strong convolutional networks while using substantially fewer computational resources to train. [E:arxiv:2010.11929:abstract:claim:e28076c4f341] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:4:8ad541081adb:claim:15e2b55a7b53]

assertions.source_quote: The original ViT problem is image classification rather than dense prediction. An image is divided into coarse patches, embedded into a sequence, and processed by standard Transformer self-attention and MLP layers without relying on convolutional feature extraction. CNN backbones instead encode locality, weight sharing and translation equivariance directly through convolution kernels; deep residual CNNs such as ResNet made very deep convolutional stacks trainable through skip connections and became common components for classification, detection and segmentation. Thus, the relevant comparison is not simply attention versus convolution as isolated operators, but two backbone families with different built-in spatial priors, feature resolutions, scaling behavior, and interfaces to downstream heads. assertions.source_quote: Training data is a central scope condition. The original ViT evidence depends on large-scale pretraining followed by transfer, whereas later work reports that the practical optimization burden of plain ViT can be substantial: ConTNet, for example, motivates its convolution-transformer design by noting ViT's need for specialized training settings or hundreds of millions of pretraining images. A broad benchmark study also cautions against treating ViT popularity as a universal winner across applications: across more than 1,500 training runs spanning classification, detection, out-of-distribution generalization and other tasks, supervised CNN backbones pretrained on large datasets performed best on most tasks among the models considered. That result concerns the particular pretrained model suite and benchmarks, not an architecture-independent law. assertions.source_quote: For this review, the organizing choice is a four-criterion comparison rather than a universal taxonomy: (1) basic visual operator and inductive bias, (2) feature geometry for downstream heads, (3) pretraining and representation objective, and (4) evaluation task and deployment constraint. These criteria separate questions that are often conflated: a model may be a pure Transformer by operator, a single-scale classifier by feature geometry, and a strong transferred model only under a particular large-data pretraining regime. The labels “ViT” and “CNN” therefore identify architecture families, not guaranteed accuracy, efficiency, or task suitability. assertions.source_quote: The second criterion is feature geometry. Original ViT's columnar patch sequence yields one principal representation for classification and, in the PVT analysis, a single-scale, low-resolution output map that is awkward to connect directly to detection or segmentation heads. CNN-style pyramid backbones and adapted Transformers instead expose multi-stage or multi-scale features; PVT adds a progressive shrinking pyramid and spatial-reduction attention, HVT progressively pools tokens similarly to CNN downsampling, and ViT-CoMer adds a multi-receptive-field convolutional feature pyramid. This review therefore classifies dense-prediction suitability by output resolution and scale hierarchy, not by whether the paper uses the word Transformer. CNN-style pyramid backbones and adapted Transformers instead expose multi-stage or multi-scale features; PVT adds a progressive shrinking pyramid and spatial-reduction attention, HVT progressively pools tokens similarly to CNN downsampling, and ViT-CoMer adds a multi-receptive-field convolutional feature pyramid. This review therefore classifies dense-prediction suitability by output resolution and scale hierarchy, not by whether the paper uses the word Transformer. assertions.source_quote: The third criterion keeps architecture separate from pretraining and objective. ViT-CoMer explicitly preserves the original ViT body so that open-source ViT pretrained weights can be loaded, while its added convolutional and fusion components use random initialization; it also reports stronger results when advanced ViT pretraining is used. Battle of the Backbones broadens this axis by benchmarking supervised, self-supervised, vision-language and other pretrained backbones across many tasks. CLIP-backbone studies similarly show that ViT-style and ConvNet encoders can share the same contrastive language-image objective yet produce meaningfully different representations and predictions. Consequently, “ViT versus ResNet” is under-specified unless pretraining data, supervision objective, initialization and transfer protocol are stated. assertions.source_quote: The third criterion keeps architecture separate from pretraining and objective. ViT-CoMer explicitly preserves the original ViT body so that open-source ViT pretrained weights can be loaded, while its added convolutional and fusion components use random initialization; it also reports stronger results when advanced ViT pretraining is used. Battle of the Backbones broadens this axis by benchmarking supervised, self-supervised, vision-language and other pretrained backbones across many tasks. CLIP-backbone studies similarly show that ViT-style and ConvNet encoders can share the same contrastive language-image objective yet produce meaningfully different representations and predictions. Consequently, “ViT versus ResNet” is under-specified unless pretraining data, supervision objective, initialization and transfer protocol are stated. assertions.source_quote: The fourth criterion is the target task. Image classification primarily asks for an image-level representation, whereas detection and semantic or instance segmentation require spatially localized, often multi-scale features; PVT and ViT-CoMer both motivate their designs by this mismatch between plain ViT and dense prediction. Broader backbone benchmarks add out-of-distribution generalization and other vision tasks, while high-resolution multimodal encoding introduces a different objective: compressing many image locations into a manageable number of visual tokens. Results from one task should not be reclassified as evidence for another merely because the same backbone name appears. assertions.source_quote: Efficiency must also be kept as a distinct dimension. Quadratic self-attention cost with token count, memory use, FLOPs, parameter count, inference latency and edge-device deployment are related but not interchangeable. PVT addresses high-resolution Transformer cost through shorter sequences and spatial-reduction attention; HVT pools tokens to improve scalability at comparable FLOPs; ConvLLaVA uses hierarchical ConvNeXt compression to reduce excessive visual tokens; and edge-splitting work targets latency and model size after deployment. Thus, a classification accuracy result, a token-compression result and an edge-inference result are comparable only when they report the same resource measure and operating setting. assertions.source_quote: The original Vision Transformer makes the strongest architectural departure from conventional CNN backbones: it does not use convolutional stages as its primary visual encoder. An image is split into fixed patches, each patch is linearly embedded, positional information is added, and the resulting sequence is passed through standard Transformer encoder blocks built from multi-head self-attention and MLP sublayers. Its contribution was to show that reliance on CNNs is not necessary for image classification: a pure patch-sequence Transformer can perform very well when pretrained on large data and transferred to ImageNet, CIFAR-100, VTAB and other recognition benchmarks. The applicability boundary is therefore important: the original claim is about a convolution-free classifier under large-scale pretraining and transfer, not about a universal replacement for every CNN feature pyramid or dense-prediction head. [E:arxiv:2010.11929:abstract:claim:e28076c4f341]

assertions.source_quote: The mechanism of ViT differs from a CNN in how spatial access is obtained. A CNN applies shared local kernels over a grid; its early layers have fixed local receptive fields, and broader context generally emerges as layers and downsampling stages accumulate. In ViT, self-attention lets a token aggregate information from other patch positions according to content-dependent weights. Representation analyses using CKA and attention-distance measurements find that ViT layers have a more uniform internal similarity structure than ResNet stages, and that even low ViT layers contain a mixture of attention heads with short and long average attention distances; higher ViT heads become global. This supports the architectural contrast between learned, content-dependent global mixing and the CNN's locally hard-coded, progressively expanding receptive field, without implying that global attention is always preferable for a task. assertions.source_quote: The same analyses also show that architectural difference should not be read as complete functional unrelatedness. CKA comparisons between ViT and ResNet identify portions of the networks that compute broadly similar representations, although the layer-to-stage mapping is uneven: many lower ResNet layers correspond to a smaller lower portion of ViT, while later portions map to later ViT layers. A separate unified interpretation goes further by describing vision Transformers as ConvNets with dynamic, content-dependent convolutions, allowing Transformer and dynamic-convolution design choices to be compared in one framework. assertions.source_quote: The same analyses also show that architectural difference should not be read as complete functional unrelatedness. CKA comparisons between ViT and ResNet identify portions of the networks that compute broadly similar representations, although the layer-to-stage mapping is uneven: many lower ResNet layers correspond to a smaller lower portion of ViT, while later portions map to later ViT layers. A separate unified interpretation goes further by describing vision Transformers as ConvNets with dynamic, content-dependent convolutions, allowing Transformer and dynamic-convolution design choices to be compared in one framework. That interpretation is a modeling lens rather than evidence that ViT contains ordinary static convolutions; it nevertheless weakens any simplistic claim that the two families have no exchangeable design principles. assertions.source_quote: CNN backbones represented by ResNet and ResNeXt provide the reference design against which original ViT was evaluated. Convolution kernels share weights across spatial locations and encode local visual context; ResNet's skip connections made very deep convolutional stacks practical, while multi-path and grouped convolutional designs such as Inception, ResNeXt and related architectures expanded the convolutional block design space. These networks naturally operate on image grids and commonly produce hierarchical feature maps that can feed image classifiers as well as detection and segmentation frameworks. Their inductive bias is therefore stronger than plain ViT's: locality, translation equivariance and grid hierarchy are built into the representation rather than learned largely from data. [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:4:8ad541081adb:claim:15e2b55a7b53]

assertions.source_quote: The original ViT's feature geometry is less naturally aligned with standard dense-prediction pipelines than a hierarchical CNN backbone. PVT describes ViT as a columnar network over coarse patches, designed for image classification and producing a single-scale, low-resolution output feature map. With a common patch size such as 32×32, the spatial output can be very coarse; moving to much finer patches would raise the computational and memory cost of attention, especially at detection-style image sizes around an 800-pixel shorter edge. This is a mechanism-to-task mismatch, not a statement that attention cannot solve dense prediction: it explains why directly plugging the original ViT into RetinaNet-, Mask R-CNN- or FCN-style heads is difficult without added hierarchy, resolution control or fusion. [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:2:9088148f1c89:claim:dc61f5348c17] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:3:4ed8cc57457f:claim:58348b0a1baf]

assertions.source_quote: Hierarchical Visual Transformer adopts a related but narrower adaptation for image classification. Instead of retaining a full-length patch sequence throughout inference, HVT progressively pools visual tokens, shrinking sequence length in a manner analogous to CNN feature-map downsampling. The authors report that average-pooled visual tokens are empirically more discriminative than relying on a single class token, and that token reduction creates room to scale depth, width, input resolution or patch size without proportionally increasing computation. Its contribution is therefore a scalable hierarchical pooling design for classification, with reported advantages over competitive baselines at comparable FLOPs on ImageNet and CIFAR-100. It is not the original ViT and does not by itself establish dense-prediction performance. [E:arxiv:2103.10619:abstract:claim:b63f08e2d402]

assertions.source_quote: Hierarchical Visual Transformer adopts a related but narrower adaptation for image classification. Instead of retaining a full-length patch sequence throughout inference, HVT progressively pools visual tokens, shrinking sequence length in a manner analogous to CNN feature-map downsampling. The authors report that average-pooled visual tokens are empirically more discriminative than relying on a single class token, and that token reduction creates room to scale depth, width, input resolution or patch size without proportionally increasing computation. Its contribution is therefore a scalable hierarchical pooling design for classification, with reported advantages over competitive baselines at comparable FLOPs on ImageNet and CIFAR-100. It is not the original ViT and does not by itself establish dense-prediction performance. [E:arxiv:2103.10619:abstract:claim:b63f08e2d402]

assertions.source_quote: ViT-CoMer addresses the same dense-prediction mismatch from a hybrid direction while deliberately preserving the plain ViT body. It injects a spatial pyramid of multi-receptive-field convolutional features into ViT to compensate for limited inner-patch or local interaction and for ViT's single-feature representation, and it uses a CNN–Transformer bidirectional fusion module to integrate hierarchical features across stages. A key compatibility choice is that the ViT module can directly load open-source pretrained ViT weights, while the added convolutional and fusion components are randomly initialized. The paper reports that using advanced pretrained ViT weights improves the model and positions the architecture as a feature-enhanced, pre-training-free addition on top of an available pretrained ViT rather than as a vision-specific Transformer that must discard existing ViT checkpoints. assertions.source_quote: ConTNet represents the opposite hybrid arrangement: a standard Transformer encoder is treated as a module inside a convolutional network rather than as the preserved central backbone. A feature map is divided into patches, each patch is flattened into a local sequence and processed by a standard Transformer encoder, and the resulting embeddings are reshaped back to feature maps for subsequent convolution or Transformer-encoder operations. In this design, convolutions efficiently extract local visual information while the Transformer-encoder component captures context over the patch sequence. The authors argue that embedding the Transformer encoder in a ConvNet-like architecture makes optimization more ResNet-like and reduces dependence on the extensive pretraining data or specialized training settings they associate with ViT. ConTNet is thus a conv–Transformer backbone, not evidence for either pure ViT or pure CNN superiority. assertions.source_quote: ConTNet represents the opposite hybrid arrangement: a standard Transformer encoder is treated as a module inside a convolutional network rather than as the preserved central backbone. A feature map is divided into patches, each patch is flattened into a local sequence and processed by a standard Transformer encoder, and the resulting embeddings are reshaped back to feature maps for subsequent convolution or Transformer-encoder operations. In this design, convolutions efficiently extract local visual information while the Transformer-encoder component captures context over the patch sequence. The authors argue that embedding the Transformer encoder in a ConvNet-like architecture makes optimization more ResNet-like and reduces dependence on the extensive pretraining data or specialized training settings they associate with ViT. ConTNet is thus a conv–Transformer backbone, not evidence for either pure ViT or pure CNN superiority. assertions.source_quote: Pretraining and objective are part of a backbone method, not interchangeable accessories. Original ViT's central result explicitly depends on large-scale pretraining followed by transfer to smaller or mid-sized recognition datasets. ViT-CoMer similarly separates the value of the architecture from the value of available ViT checkpoints: its plain ViT component accepts open-source pretraining, including advanced self-supervised weights, while newly added modules start from random initialization. Battle of the Backbones broadens this point by comparing supervised CNNs, self-supervised models, vision-language models and other pretrained encoders across many tasks. Consequently, a fair mechanism comparison must state whether a CNN and ViT share pretraining data, labels, objective, epoch budget, augmentation and fine-tuning protocol; otherwise an observed accuracy gap may reflect the training recipe rather than the operator alone. assertions.source_quote: Task scope is another applicability boundary. Original ViT directly targets image-level recognition, where a single aggregated representation can suffice. CNN pyramid backbones and adapted Transformers target a broader interface in which detection and segmentation heads consume localized, multi-stage feature maps. PVT motivates its entire pyramid and spatial-reduction design by the needs of object detection and semantic and instance segmentation; ViT-CoMer similarly evaluates detection, instance segmentation and semantic segmentation after adding convolutional multi-scale features. Thus, original ViT can be a strong classification backbone under the right pretraining while remaining an awkward direct backbone for dense heads, whereas a hierarchical CNN may offer a convenient feature pyramid without providing ViT's native content-dependent global token mixing. assertions.source_quote: Task scope is another applicability boundary. Original ViT directly targets image-level recognition, where a single aggregated representation can suffice. CNN pyramid backbones and adapted Transformers target a broader interface in which detection and segmentation heads consume localized, multi-stage feature maps. PVT motivates its entire pyramid and spatial-reduction design by the needs of object detection and semantic and instance segmentation; ViT-CoMer similarly evaluates detection, instance segmentation and semantic segmentation after adding convolutional multi-scale features. Thus, original ViT can be a strong classification backbone under the right pretraining while remaining an awkward direct backbone for dense heads, whereas a hierarchical CNN may offer a convenient feature pyramid without providing ViT's native content-dependent global token mixing. assertions.source_quote: The high-resolution multimodal setting introduces yet another backbone role: the visual encoder must compress an image into a manageable sequence of tokens for a large multimodal model, rather than merely produce a class label or detection feature map. ConvLLaVA replaces ViT with ConvNeXt because hierarchical convolution can compress high-resolution images into information-rich features and avoid generating excessive visual tokens; it further adapts the low-resolution-pretrained ConvNeXt for high resolution and adds a successive compression stage. At 1536×1536 input, the reported design produces 576 visual tokens and supports arbitrary aspect ratios. This supports using hierarchical CNN structure for token-budgeted encoding, but it is not a like-for-like ImageNet accuracy comparison with original ViT because the task, decoder and resolution regime differ. assertions.source_quote: The broad empirical literature also cautions against treating architecture type as a sufficient selection rule. Battle of the Backbones benchmarked a diverse set of more than 1,500 trained models across classification, detection, out-of-distribution generalization and additional computer-vision tasks, and found that supervised CNN backbones pretrained on large training sets performed best on most tasks among the models considered. It also found self-supervised backbones competitive in apples-to-apples comparisons when architecture and pretraining-dataset size were matched. This is evidence about a specific model suite, pretraining menu and benchmark collection; it does not overturn ViT's original large-data transfer result, nor does it prove that CNNs are intrinsically superior. [E:arxiv:2310.19909:abstract:claim:65d7d13e0881] [E:arxiv:2010.11929:abstract:claim:e28076c4f341]

It also found self-supervised backbones competitive in apples-to-apples comparisons when architecture and pretraining-dataset size were matched. This is evidence about a specific model suite, pretraining menu and benchmark collection; it does not overturn ViT's original large-data transfer result, nor does it prove that CNNs are intrinsically superior. assertions.source_quote: Mechanism-level evidence and application-level evidence therefore lead to a nuanced division of labor. assertions.source_quote: The experimental comparison should be read by matched task and training regime, not by pooling all ViT and CNN numbers. The original ViT paper's central evidence is transfer after large-scale pretraining: on ImageNet, CIFAR-100, VTAB and related recognition benchmarks, a pure Transformer over image patches attained excellent results relative to state-of-the-art convolutional networks and was reported to require substantially fewer computational resources to train. That result supports the viability of a convolution-free image classifier under the paper's large-data transfer setting; it does not provide a matched claim that the same original ViT beats ResNet-style backbones on detection or segmentation. assertions.source_quote: Representation analyses provide a second, non-accuracy comparison under controlled model inspection rather than a leaderboard ranking. CKA heatmaps show that ViT and ResNet propagate representations differently: ViT has a more uniform, grid-like similarity structure and greater similarity between lower and higher layers, whereas ResNet representations separate more clearly into lower and higher stages. In cross-model CKA comparisons, the lower half of a 60-layer ResNet is broadly similar to about the lowest quarter of the compared ViT, the upper half of ResNet to roughly the next third of ViT, and the final third of ViT is less similar to ResNet. These are structural correspondences for the analyzed models and layers, not a claim that the architectures have identical feature hierarchies. assertions.source_quote: Attention-distance measurements add a task-independent mechanism comparison on 5,000 datapoints in the cited analysis. Even the lowest ViT self-attention layers contain heads with both short and long average query-to-attended-location distances, while higher layers have global heads; by contrast, early CNN layers are hard-coded to local receptive fields. This experimentally supports the distinction between ViT's content-dependent mixing across patch locations and a CNN's fixed local filters that expand context through depth. It does not establish that global attention yields higher accuracy unless the dataset, head, pretraining and compute budget are matched. assertions.source_quote: The clearest dense-prediction comparison in the selected sources is PVT against CNN backbones, not original ViT against CNNs. assertions.source_quote: ConTNet provides a hybrid comparison oriented toward classification optimization and dense transfer. The paper reports that ConT-M exceeds ResNet50 top-1 accuracy on ImageNet by 1.6% while saving almost 25% relative computational cost, and that it improves over ResNet50 by around 3% in dense prediction when used with FCOS and Mask R-CNN. It also argues that ConTNet can be optimized more like ordinary ConvNets and does not require the training tricks associated with DeiT or the very large pretraining data used by ViT. These findings compare a specific conv–Transformer block design with ResNet50 under the paper's protocols; they are not an original-ViT-versus-CNN controlled benchmark. assertions.source_quote: HVT gives a classification-scaling comparison for a hierarchical token-pooling Transformer. The authors report that, at comparable FLOPs, HVT outperforms competitive baselines on ImageNet and CIFAR-100, and that average-pooled visual tokens are empirically more discriminative than a single class token in their experiments. The relevant resource axis here is FLOPs under the reported classification settings; the paper does not provide the latency, parameter count, detection performance or segmentation performance needed to compare HVT with CNN backbones on those dimensions. [E:arxiv:2103.10619:abstract:claim:b63f08e2d402]

assertions.source_quote: Across broad backbone choices, Battle of the Backbones is the most task-diverse selected benchmark but its conclusion is suite-specific. The study ran more than 1,500 training runs over classification, object detection, out-of-distribution generalization and other computer-vision tasks, comparing pretrained models that included supervised CNNs, self-supervised backbones, vision-language models and the Stable Diffusion backbone. Among the models considered, large-dataset supervised CNN backbones performed best on most tasks; in apples-to-apples comparisons with the same architectures and similarly sized pretraining datasets, self-supervised backbones were highly competitive. This does not contradict original ViT's large-data transfer claim, because model menu, pretraining data, objective and task coverage differ. [E:arxiv:2310.19909:abstract:claim:65d7d13e0881] [E:arxiv:2010.11929:abstract:claim:e28076c4f341]

assertions.source_quote: The CLIP study shows that matching the training objective still leaves architecture-dependent representation effects. ViT-style and ConvNet encoders such as ResNets were trained with CLIP using the same data and objective, yet their classifications differed substantially; representation normalization caused large performance variations, informed selection among complementary backbone predictions could yield an improvement of more than 20% in the authors' analysis, and combining predictions from multiple backbones improved performance by up to 6.34%. These are prediction-complementarity results under the studied CLIP protocols, not a direct accuracy or efficiency ranking of original ViT and CNN backbones. [E:arxiv:2312.14400:abstract:claim:a57f112285cc]

assertions.source_quote: High-resolution multimodal encoding requires a separate comparison because its primary metric is token compression for a downstream LMM rather than ImageNet accuracy or COCO AP. ConvLLaVA replaces ViT with an adapted hierarchical ConvNeXt encoder and reports that 1536×1536 images produce 576 visual tokens while supporting arbitrary aspect ratios. The cited abstract also reports competitive performance with state-of-the-art models on mainstream benchmarks, but without matched model sizes, latency, training data or exact benchmark tables in the available source quote, this should not be converted into a general CNN-over-ViT ranking. assertions.source_quote: Taken together, the experiments support a conditional comparison rather than a universal winner. Original ViT is strongly supported as a convolution-free transfer classifier under large-scale pretraining; CNN backbones remain competitive or superior in broad benchmark suites and provide natural hierarchical feature maps; PVT, HVT, ViT-CoMer and ConTNet improve or adapt Transformer behavior by introducing pyramids, pooling, convolution, fusion or easier optimization. Any numerical ranking across these studies is invalid where the architecture is not the original ViT, the task changes from classification to dense prediction or multimodal tokenization, or pretraining data, objective, parameters, FLOPs, detector and input resolution are not matched. assertions.source_quote: The first open problem is that the original ViT's strongest result carries a data and optimization condition that CNN backbones often do not require to the same degree. ViT's convolution-free patch sequence was shown to work very well after large-scale pretraining and transfer, but later hybrid work explicitly motivates its design by the practical burden of specialized training settings or hundreds of millions of pretraining images. This means practitioners cannot infer from ViT's benchmark success that a randomly initialized, modest-dataset ViT will match a well-tuned ResNet under the same schedule. The unresolved issue is not merely whether Transformers can learn visual locality, but how much data, augmentation, regularization, optimization tuning and compute are needed before the weaker built-in visual bias becomes a net advantage rather than a training cost. assertions.source_quote: The original ViT also leaves a concrete dense-prediction interface problem. PVT identifies two direct obstacles: ViT's columnar coarse-patch representation produces a single-scale, low-resolution output, and reducing patch size to obtain finer spatial maps raises attention computation and memory cost at typical detection resolutions. These limitations matter because detection and segmentation heads need localized features, often at several stages and receptive-field scales. The implication is not that Transformers are unsuitable for dense prediction, but that the original ViT classifier cannot be treated as a drop-in replacement for a CNN feature pyramid without changing resolution, hierarchy, token budget or the downstream head itself. assertions.source_quote: Later adaptations confirm rather than eliminate this trade-off. PVT adds fine initial patches, progressive sequence shrinking and spatial-reduction attention; HVT pools tokens to shorten the sequence; and ViT-CoMer adds convolutional multi-receptive-field features plus CNN–Transformer fusion to address limited local interaction and single-scale representation. Each method improves suitability for scaling or dense tasks, but each also changes the original ViT mechanism, adds design components, or introduces modules that cannot simply inherit all pretrained weights. PVT adds fine initial patches, progressive sequence shrinking and spatial-reduction attention; HVT pools tokens to shorten the sequence; and ViT-CoMer adds convolutional multi-receptive-field features plus CNN–Transformer fusion to address limited local interaction and single-scale representation. Each method improves suitability for scaling or dense tasks, but each also changes the original ViT mechanism, adds design components, or introduces modules that cannot simply inherit all pretrained weights. Thus, an open design problem remains: obtain high-resolution, multi-scale, local-and-global features without sacrificing the simplicity, checkpoint compatibility and pure-sequence pretraining advantages of original ViT. assertions.source_quote: Mechanism analyses also leave unresolved questions about why the two backbone families behave differently. CKA shows that ViT has a more uniform internal representation structure and greater similarity across lower and higher layers, while ResNet representations separate more distinctly into stages; attention-distance analysis finds local and global heads even in early ViT layers, unlike early CNN layers with fixed local receptive fields. These observations explain differences in information propagation and global access, but they do not specify when global mixing improves robustness, sample efficiency or downstream accuracy. A dynamic-convolution interpretation offers a unified design lens, yet it does not collapse static convolution and self-attention into identical operators or determine which inductive bias is preferable under limited data. assertions.source_quote: Resource accounting remains fragmented. Self-attention cost grows with token count, and PVT and HVT target sequence length and FLOPs, but parameter count, FLOPs, peak memory, inference latency and edge-device footprint are not interchangeable measures. ConvLLaVA addresses a different bottleneck—excessive visual tokens in high-resolution multimodal models—by using a hierarchical ConvNeXt encoder and reports 576 visual tokens at 1536×1536 resolution; edge ViT work instead reports deployment-time latency and size reductions through splitting and pruning. These results cannot be combined into one efficiency ranking unless hardware, batch size, resolution, token count, precision and decoder are matched. A major practical problem is therefore reporting end-to-end resource use under the target application rather than relying on one proxy such as FLOPs. assertions.source_quote: Hybrid architectures show promise but introduce their own optimization and attribution questions. ConTNet embeds a standard Transformer encoder inside a convolutional feature-map network and reports easier ConvNet-like optimization, higher ImageNet accuracy than ResNet50 at lower reported compute, and improved FCOS and Mask R-CNN results. ViT-CoMer instead starts from pretrained ViT and injects convolutional features. These designs make it difficult to attribute gains cleanly to global attention, local convolution, hierarchy, pretrained weights or optimization stability. assertions.source_quote: Finally, task transfer remains the central boundary on any broad conclusion. Original ViT was designed for image classification and demonstrated strong large-data transfer to recognition benchmarks; CNN pyramids have a natural interface for detection and segmentation; ConvNeXt-based ConvLLaVA is used to compress high-resolution images for multimodal models; and broad benchmark suites include out-of-distribution generalization and many other tasks. Accuracy on one task does not establish suitability for another, and missing evidence in the selected papers does not prove a field-wide gap. unsupported_claims.source_quote: The comparison also changes when the target is dense prediction. The original ViT's columnar, single-scale and relatively low-resolution patch features were designed primarily for classification; PVT documents that directly using such features for detection and segmentation at common high-resolution inputs is difficult because the output map is single-scale and low-resolution, while finer patches sharply increase computational and memory cost. unsupported_claims.source_quote: ConTNet represents the opposite hybrid arrangement: a standard Transformer encoder is treated as a module inside a convolutional network rather than as the preserved central backbone. A feature map is divided into patches, each patch is flattened into a local sequence and processed by a standard Transformer encoder, and the resulting embeddings are reshaped back to feature maps for subsequent convolution or Transformer-encoder operations. In this design, convolutions efficiently extract local visual information while the Transformer-encoder component captures context over the patch sequence. The authors argue that embedding the Transformer encoder in a ConvNet-like architecture makes optimization more ResNet-like and reduces dependence on the extensive pretraining data or specialized training settings they associate with ViT. ConTNet is thus a conv–Transformer backbone, not evidence for either pure ViT or pure CNN superiority. unsupported_claims.source_quote: Pretraining and objective are part of a backbone method, not interchangeable accessories. Original ViT's central result explicitly depends on large-scale pretraining followed by transfer to smaller or mid-sized recognition datasets. ViT-CoMer similarly separates the value of the architecture from the value of available ViT checkpoints: its plain ViT component accepts open-source pretraining, including advanced self-supervised weights, while newly added modules start from random initialization. Battle of the Backbones broadens this point by comparing supervised CNNs, self-supervised models, vision-language models and other pretrained encoders across many tasks. Consequently, a fair mechanism comparison must state whether a CNN and ViT share pretraining data, labels, objective, epoch budget, augmentation and fine-tuning protocol; otherwise an observed accuracy gap may reflect the training recipe rather than the operator alone. unsupported_claims.source_quote: Task scope is another applicability boundary. Original ViT directly targets image-level recognition, where a single aggregated representation can suffice. CNN pyramid backbones and adapted Transformers target a broader interface in which detection and segmentation heads consume localized, multi-stage feature maps. PVT motivates its entire pyramid and spatial-reduction design by the needs of object detection and semantic and instance segmentation; ViT-CoMer similarly evaluates detection, instance segmentation and semantic segmentation after adding convolutional multi-scale features. Thus, original ViT can be a strong classification backbone under the right pretraining while remaining an awkward direct backbone for dense heads, whereas a hierarchical CNN may offer a convenient feature pyramid without providing ViT's native content-dependent global token mixing. unsupported_claims.source_quote: The high-resolution multimodal setting introduces yet another backbone role: the visual encoder must compress an image into a manageable sequence of tokens for a large multimodal model, rather than merely produce a class label or detection feature map. ConvLLaVA replaces ViT with ConvNeXt because hierarchical convolution can compress high-resolution images into information-rich features and avoid generating excessive visual tokens; it further adapts the low-resolution-pretrained ConvNeXt for high resolution and adds a successive compression stage. At 1536×1536 input, the reported design produces 576 visual tokens and supports arbitrary aspect ratios. This supports using hierarchical CNN structure for token-budgeted encoding, but it is not a like-for-like ImageNet accuracy comparison with original ViT because the task, decoder and resolution regime differ. unsupported_claims.source_quote: The broad empirical literature also cautions against treating architecture type as a sufficient selection rule. Battle of the Backbones benchmarked a diverse set of more than 1,500 trained models across classification, detection, out-of-distribution generalization and additional computer-vision tasks, and found that supervised CNN backbones pretrained on large training sets performed best on most tasks among the models considered. It also found self-supervised backbones competitive in apples-to-apples comparisons when architecture and pretraining-dataset size were matched. This is evidence about a specific model suite, pretraining menu and benchmark collection; it does not overturn ViT's original large-data transfer result, nor does it prove that CNNs are intrinsically superior.
